title: Predict The Presence of Data Center(s) in a County
author: Logan Rosell

## Goal
To get a sense of how predictive each of our available x variables are of whether a county does or does not have data centers we will create a simple Logistic Regression model including all variables. While we do know which counties have data centers in them as of 2023, we do not know what year any specific county started having data centers. We also cannot be sure that counties which are not included in the list of those with data centers in 2023 did not previously have a data center at some point during our analysis window which was closed down before 2023 and thus not included in our list of counties with data centers.

def load_table(table_name, engine):

    df.columns = [str(col) for col in df.columns]
    return df

## Create Table for models

### Helper Functions

```{python}
def combine_dfs(base_df, dfs_to_join):
    out_df = base_df.copy()

    for i, df in enumerate(dfs_to_join):
        if "county_id" not in df.columns:
            raise ValueError(f"No `county_id` column found in dfs_to_join[{i}]")

        # Make sure all tables only have one row per county
        dupes = df["county_id"][df["county_id"].duplicated()].unique()
        if len(dupes) > 0:
            raise ValueError(f"dfs_to_join[{i}] is not unique on `county_id`. Problematic Counties: {list(dupes)}")

        out_df = pd.merge(out_df, df, how = "left", on = "county_id", validate = "one_to_one")

    missing_summary_table = (
        out_df.isna()
        .mean()
        .sort_values(ascending = False)
        .rename("missing_share")
        .reset_index()
        .rename(columns={"index":"column"})
    )

    print("Missing Summary: \n", missing_summary_table)

    return out_df
```

```{python}
# slice df to specific year
def return_specific_year(df, year):
    assert"year" in df.columns, "data frame does not have a year column"
    year = int(year)
    sliced_df = df[df["year"]==year]
    sliced_df = sliced_df.drop(columns = ["year"])
    return sliced_df
```

# Make applicable columns per-capita
def make_per_capita(df, per_capita_cols):

    for col in per_capita_cols:
        df[f"{col}_per_capita"] = df[col] / df["population"]

    df = df.drop(columns=per_capita_cols)
    return df

## EDA
 
 ```{python}
# compare the mean value for all features between counties with and without datacenters
dc_counties =  mega_df[mega_df["has_datacenter"]==1]
dc_counties = dc_counties.drop(columns = ["county_id", "has_datacenter"])
dc_county_means = dc_counties.mean().to_frame()
dc_county_means["has_dc"] = "no"
dc_county_means.columns = ["mean", "has_dc"]

non_dc_counties =  mega_df[mega_df["has_datacenter"]==0]
non_dc_counties = non_dc_counties.drop(columns = ["county_id", "has_datacenter"])
non_dc_county_means = non_dc_counties.mean().to_frame()
non_dc_county_means["has_dc"] = "yes"
non_dc_county_means.columns = ["mean", "has_dc"]

comparing_means_df = pd.concat([dc_county_means, non_dc_county_means], axis=0)
comparing_means_df = comparing_means_df.reset_index().rename(columns={"index": "feature"})

feature_list = comparing_means_df["feature"].unique()

for i in feature_list:
    sns.barplot(
        x = "feature",
        y = "mean",
        hue = "has_dc",
        data = comparing_means_df[comparing_means_df["feature"]==i]
    )
    plt.show()

 ```


Check for statistically significantly different means between counties with and without data centers using the Mann-Whitney U Test. Because checking 40 different features at the same time increases the risk of finding a fase-positive we are using the Benjamini-Hochberg correction. 
```{python}
# Check for statistically significantly different means between counties with and without data centers using the Mann-Whitney U Test

dc_group = mega_df[mega_df["has_datacenter"] == 1]
non_dc_group = mega_df[mega_df["has_datacenter"] == 0]

# all numeric columns
features = list(mega_df.columns)[2:]

results = []

for col in features:
    g1 = dc_group[col].dropna()
    g2 = non_dc_group[col].dropna()
    
    median_dc = g1.median()
    median_non_dc = g2.median()
    
    stat, p_val = stats.mannwhitneyu(g1, g2, alternative="two-sided")
    
    results.append({
        "feature": col,
        "median_with_dc": median_dc,
        "median_no_dc": median_non_dc,
        "p_value": p_val
    })

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results)

# Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction
reject, p_corrected, _, _ = multipletests(results_df["p_value"], alpha=0.05, method="fdr_bh")

results_df["p_adjusted"] = p_corrected
results_df["is_significant"] = reject
results_df = results_df.sort_values(by="p_adjusted")
```

## Models

### Logistic Regression

```{python}
# set up train and test datasets
independent_x_vars_df = independent_x_vars_df.dropna()

y = independent_x_vars_df["has_datacenter"]
X = independent_x_vars_df.drop(columns = ["county_id", "has_datacenter"])


X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=57, stratify=y)
```


```{python}
# scale features since they have very different ranges
scaler = StandardScaler()

X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train.values)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test.values)
```


Using class_weight='balanced' since the vast majority of counties do not have a datacenter meaning that if we don't balance the training data it model will tend to just guess that all counties don't have a data center.
```{python}
# train the model
log_reg = LogisticRegression(random_state=57, class_weight='balanced')
log_reg.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
```


```{python}
# evaluate model performance

y_pred_train = log_reg.predict(X_train_scaled)
train_acc = sum(y_pred_train == y_train) / len(y_train)
print(f"Training Accuracy: {train_acc:.4f}")

y_pred_test = log_reg.predict(X_test_scaled)

ConfusionMatrixDisplay(
    confusion_matrix=confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_test), 
    display_labels=log_reg.classes_
).plot()

plt.show()
```

#### Interpreting Logistic Model Results

```{python}
coef_df = pd.DataFrame({
    'Variable': X.columns,
    'Coefficient': log_reg.coef_[0]
})

# Add the intercept
intercept_df = pd.DataFrame({'Variable': ['Intercept'], 'Coefficient': log_reg.intercept_})
coef_df = pd.concat([intercept_df, coef_df], ignore_index=True)

print(coef_df)
```


A Durbin-Watson score = 2 indicates perfect independence of the residuals (assumption of Logistic Regression). A score < 2 indicates postive autocorrelation and a score > 2 indicates negative autocorreclation. 
```{python}
# Check for independce of errors
pred_probabilities = log_reg.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]

residuals = y - pred_probabilities

dw_stat = durbin_watson(residuals)
print("Durbin-Watson:", dw_stat)
```
